result:
Don't split yet: restructure it as a modular monolith first, and move to micro-frontends only if independent deployment is still the bottleneck afterwards.

Micro-frontends buy you one thing: each team ships on its own schedule without waiting on anyone else's build, tests or release train. You pay for that with runtime integration complexity (Module Federation or similar, shared-dependency version skew, duplicated bundles, slower page loads), harder cross-cutting changes (design system, auth, routing and React upgrades become multi-team migrations), and a platform burden that usually needs dedicated owners.

Five teams is in the range where most of the pain comes from unclear boundaries and slow CI rather than from the single deployable, and those are cheaper to fix directly:

1. Split the app into per-team packages in a monorepo (Nx or Turborepo) with CODEOWNERS and lint-enforced import boundaries.
2. Add affected-only builds and tests with remote caching so CI time tracks the size of the change, not the size of the app.
3. Decouple release from deploy with feature flags and continuous deployment from main, plus route-level code splitting.

That gets you most of the autonomy at a fraction of the cost, and the boundaries it creates are the same seams you would cut along later, so the work is not wasted.

Splitting is the right call if, after that, teams are still regularly blocked by each other's releases, need different release cadences or compliance isolation, or one area needs to be on a different stack. In that case, extract only the one or two domains that are hurting rather than all five.
